questions.title: Why does multiplying a pretrained weight matrix by an orthogonal matrix preserve neuron angles?
questions.question_body:
I'm reading the BOFT/OFT paper, where a pretrained layer \(W^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}\) is updated to \(R W^0\) with \(R\) orthogonal. The paper says this preserves the pairwise angles between neurons, where each neuron is a column of \(W^0\). I can see that for two columns \(w_i^0\) and \(w_j^0\),
\[
(Rw_i^0)^\top (Rw_j^0) = (w_i^0)^\top R^\top R w_j^0 = (w_i^0)^\top w_j^0,
\]
so dot products and norms are preserved. But I am still unsure whether the paper is talking about preserving the geometry of columns, rows, or activations, especially since the forward pass is written as \(z = (R W^0)^\top x\).

questions.title: Why is the orthogonal update applied on the left as \(R W^0\) instead of on the right as \(W^0 R\)?
questions.question_body: In the paper, the finetuned weight is \(R W^0\), not \(W^0 R\). If \(W^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}\), then left multiplication rotates the input-side coordinates, while right multiplication would mix output neurons. The paper motivates OFT by saying it preserves pairwise angles between neurons and identifies neurons with columns of \(W^0\), so I think left multiplication is deliberate. Can someone explain clearly what quantity would be preserved by \(W^0 R\) instead, and why \(R W^0\) is the natural choice here?

questions.title: How does the Cayley parameterization used in OFT/BOFT guarantee orthogonality in practice?
questions.question_body:
The paper parameterizes the orthogonal matrix as
\[
R = (I + Q)(I - Q)^{-1}, \quad Q = -Q^\top.
\]
I understand the usual algebra showing that \(R^\top R = I\), but I am confused about the practical details. Is \(I - Q\) always invertible for a real skew-symmetric \(Q\)? Also, does the Cayley transform represent every orthogonal matrix, or only those without eigenvalue \(-1\)? If it is not surjective onto the full orthogonal group, why is it still a good parameterization for finetuning?

questions.title: In the paper's information-transmission view, when does a path in the factor graph actually imply a nonzero matrix entry?
questions.question_body: The paper interprets a factorization \(R = B_m \cdots B_1\) as information transmission on a grid, where nonzero entries in each \(B_i\) are edges between adjacent levels. I understand that if there is no path from source node \(j\) to target node \(i\), then \(R_{ij} = 0\). But is the converse always true? If there is at least one path, couldn't contributions from different paths cancel numerically so that \(R_{ij} = 0\) anyway? I am trying to understand whether the graph argument is exact, or whether it only describes the support pattern generically while ignoring measure-zero cancellations.

questions.title: Why does a sparse orthogonal matrix with exactly \(d\) nonzero entries have to be a signed permutation matrix?
questions.question_body: In the parameter-counting discussion, the paper says that for a \(d \times d\) orthogonal matrix, the minimum \(d\) edges needed for a bijection between adjacent levels should not be counted as trainable, because with exactly \(d\) nonzero entries those values can only be \(\pm 1\). I do not immediately see why orthogonality forces this. Is the claim that any real orthogonal matrix with one nonzero per row and one nonzero per column must be a signed permutation matrix? If so, could someone show the argument explicitly?

questions.title: Can someone work out a concrete butterfly factorization example for \(d = 4\) or \(d = 8\)?
questions.question_body:
I am having trouble visualizing the recursive definition
\[
B(d) = \tilde{B}(d,d)\tilde{B}(d,d/2)\cdots \tilde{B}(d,2)
\]
and the butterfly factor
\[
B^F(k) = \begin{bmatrix}
\operatorname{diag}(d_1) & \operatorname{diag}(d_2) \\
\operatorname{diag}(d_3) & \operatorname{diag}(d_4)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Could someone write out the actual sparsity pattern for \(d=4\) or \(d=8\), show the individual factors, and explain why the product becomes dense even though each factor is sparse?

questions.title: What do the two BOFT hyperparameters \(m\) and \(b\) actually control?
questions.question_body: The notation in the paper confused me. It defines \(R(m,b)\) using block butterfly components \(\tilde{B}_{(d,i)}^b\), and then says BOFT with \(R(m,b/2)\) is denoted as BOFT\((m,b)\). It also states that BOFT\((1,b)\) reduces to block-diagonal OFT with block size \(b\), and BOFT\((\log (2d/b), b)\) yields a dense orthogonal matrix. I am not sure whether \(b\) is the butterfly block size, half-block size, or the size of the orthogonal submatrix being parameterized. Can someone translate this notation into a simple description of what increasing \(m\) or \(b\) does to density, expressivity, and parameter count?

questions.title: How is the BOFT parameter count \(\frac{1}{2}(b-1)dm\) derived?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that BOFT\((m,b)\) uses \(\frac{1}{2}(b-1)dm\) effective trainable parameters for a layer of size \(d \times n\). I want to understand where this count comes from. My guess is that each butterfly component contains \(d/(2b)\) blocks of size \(2b \times 2b\), but I am mixing up the number of free parameters in a full orthogonal matrix, in a skew-symmetric matrix, and in a Cayley parameterization. Could someone derive the formula step by step?

questions.title: Why does BOFT subsume block-diagonal OFT as a special case?
questions.question_body: The paper says BOFT generalizes OFT and that BOFT\((1,b)\) is exactly block-diagonal OFT with block size \(b\). I do not see this immediately because BOFT is introduced as a product of butterfly components, while OFT is described as a single block-diagonal orthogonal matrix. Is the idea that when \(m=1\), the only factor is already block diagonal, so nothing is mixed across blocks? If so, how do the block sizes in the BOFT notation line up exactly with the block sizes in OFT?

questions.title: Does left multiplication by an orthogonal matrix preserve only the spectral norm, or all singular values of \(W^0\)?
questions.question_body: In the spectral properties section, the paper says OFT/BOFT preserve the spectral norm of the pretrained weight matrix because the finetuned weight is \(R W^0\) with \(R\) orthogonal. But for rectangular \(W^0\), left multiplication by an orthogonal matrix should leave the entire singular value spectrum unchanged, not just the largest singular value. Is the stronger statement true here? If yes, why does the paper emphasize spectral norm preservation specifically instead of saying that all singular values are preserved?

questions.title: What exactly is more expressive about BOFT than OFT with the same block size?
questions.question_body: The paper states in Theorem 1 that BOFT is more expressive than OFT with the same block size, and the approximation experiment seems to support that. My current intuition is that a single block-diagonal OFT can never create interactions across blocks, while multiple butterfly factors can mix coordinates across blocks through structured permutations and local orthogonal transforms. Is that the formal reason? Is there a precise inclusion relation between the set of matrices representable by block-diagonal OFT and the set representable by BOFT for fixed \(b\)?

questions.title: Why might a more expressive finetuning family perform worse than a more constrained one?
questions.question_body: The paper says that full finetuning, despite being more expressive, often performs worse than a structured method like BOFT, and that the key trade-off is expressivity versus regularity. I understand the general bias-variance intuition, but I am struggling to connect it to this particular parameterization. What inductive bias does the butterfly structure introduce beyond simply using fewer parameters? Is the claim mainly about preserving pretrained geometry and singular values, or is there a more specific reason why FFT-like sparse mixing patterns might generalize better on downstream tasks?

questions.title: How is 'multiplicative dropout' in BOFT analogous to standard dropout?
questions.question_body: For LoRA, standard dropout is applied to the additive low-rank update. BOFT instead randomly chooses some butterfly components and some diagonal blocks within them, and replaces those blocks by identity matrices. I can see why this keeps the update multiplicative, but I do not understand the analogy with ordinary dropout. In standard dropout, activations or weights are zeroed and often rescaled so that the expectation is preserved. In BOFT, replacing a block with identity seems more like skipping part of the transformation than zeroing it. Is there an expectation-preserving interpretation here, or is this mainly a heuristic regularizer?

questions.title: What can and cannot be concluded from the paper's information-transmission framework?
questions.question_body: The paper says the framework is useful because, for designing the factorization, 'we only care about the non-zero trainable elements of \(R\) and their specific values do not matter.' This is the part I find most questionable. The actual numerical values of the orthogonal factors seem crucial for optimization and for how well the final matrix approximates a useful transformation. Is the graph view meant only to design sparsity patterns that make dense support possible, rather than to analyze approximation quality or training dynamics? I would like to understand the exact scope of what this framework explains and what it does not.
